claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films or nanoribbons contain nanoscale grain boundaries, interfacial strain, and a high density of structural defects.
Localized interfacial strain and defect-induced magnetic anisotropy create a broadened distribution of magnetic exchange interactions.
The broadened exchange-interaction distribution governs the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-field cooling cycles.
Heat-transfer rates are limited by the nanoscale geometry of these films or nanoribbons.
A mild post-deposition anneal can relieve interfacial strain and reduce defect density.
The controlled intervention is annealing at approximately 300°C for 10–30 minutes in argon.
This annealing treatment can avoid phase separation or other unwanted microstructural changes.
Relaxing strain and reducing defects will homogenize magnetic exchange interactions.
Reducing defects will reduce domain-wall pinning.
Homogenized magnetic interactions will sharpen the magnetic transition.
Reduced domain-wall pinning will diminish magnetic hysteresis.
Reduced defect scattering will improve local thermal connectivity and mitigate nanoscale heat-transfer limitations.
Annealed samples will exhibit a sharper magnetic-entropy-change peak near the magnetic transition than as-deposited samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit lower coercivity and a smaller hysteresis loop than as-deposited samples.
Annealing will improve cooling-cycle consistency by making heat-transfer limitations less pronounced.
The as-deposited baseline has a broadened and weakened magnetocaloric response and larger hysteresis because of inhomogeneous strain and high defect density.
The proposed intervention is applicable under applied fields of at most 1 T.
The relevant magnetic transition lies roughly within 100–300 K.
The annealing temperature must remain below the threshold for phase separation or other unwanted microstructural changes.
